_comment: CliniX respiratory skills - history and systemic examination. Shared across COPD, asthma, pneumonia, effusion, bronchiectasis and ILD. A disease adds emphasis (what to expect) rather than copying the skill.

skill.hx.resp.dyspnea.title: Breathlessness
skill.hx.resp.dyspnea.oneLine: Grade it against an activity, never against an adjective
skill.hx.resp.dyspnea.why: Breathlessness is the symptom that tracks disease severity and predicts prognosis, but only if it is anchored to something measurable. 'Moderate breathlessness' is uninterpretable and unrepeatable; 'stops after 100 metres on level ground' can be compared with the same patient in six months and with any other patient in the world.

asks.text: When did you first notice you were getting short of breath? Months or years, not days, in chronic disease.
What can you do now before you have to stop, and what could you do a year ago?

Grade it: breathless on strenuous exercise only (mMRC 0); hurrying or a slight hill (1); walks slower than others of the same age, or stops for breath at own pace on the level (2); stops after about 100 metres or a few minutes on the level (3); too breathless to leave the house or breathless on dressing (4).
Is it worse lying flat, and do you wake at night short of breath?
Is it constant, or does it come in attacks? What brings an attack on?
Are arm activities above shoulder height particularly bad?

skill.hx.resp.dyspnea.practice: Take a breathlessness history from a partner and finish with an mMRC grade you can defend. If you cannot name the grade, you have not asked enough.
pitfalls: Accepting 'I get breathless' without anchoring it to a distance, a number of stairs or a specific task.
Not asking what the patient could do a year ago, which is what reveals the rate of decline.
Missing orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, which point towards a cardiac contribution that often coexists with COPD.
Recording only the current grade and not the tempo, so an acute-on-chronic deterioration is invisible.

probes.q: What does mMRC grade 3 mean?
probes.a: Stops for breath after walking about 100 metres or after a few minutes on level ground.

probes.q: Why ask what the patient could do a year ago?
probes.a: It establishes the rate of decline, which distinguishes slowly progressive chronic disease from a recent, faster deterioration.

probes.q: A COPD patient reports arm activity above shoulder height is disproportionately hard. Why?
probes.a: Those activities recruit the accessory muscles that a hyperinflated patient already depends on for breathing, and they fix the shoulder girdle. Tasks that allow the arms to brace, such as pushing a trolley, are better tolerated.

rubric.text: Establishes onset and duration
Grades breathlessness against a specific activity
Compares current function with the past
Asks about orthopnoea and PND

teach.heading: Breathlessness is a sensation, not a measurement
teach.body:
Dyspnoea is the patient's own uncomfortable awareness of their breathing. It is subjective, which is exactly why you must anchor it to something you can measure.

A patient can be severely hypoxaemic and not feel breathless, and can feel desperately breathless with normal saturations. Never let the oximeter overrule the history, or the other way round.
teach.note: This is why 'moderate breathlessness' is a useless phrase. It cannot be compared with the same patient in six months, or with anyone else.

teach.heading: Why the patient feels it
teach.body: Knowing the mechanism tells you what to ask next, because each one comes with its own set of questions.

rows: Increased work of breathing, airflow obstruction
Pulmonary oedema, embolism, congestion. Gives rapid shallow breathing

teach.heading: Grade it against an activity
teach.body: Convert the sensation into a number you can defend. The mMRC scale does this with one question: what makes you stop?

points.d: Breathless only on strenuous exercise.
Short of breath hurrying on the flat, or walking up a slight hill.
Walks slower than others of the same age, or stops for breath walking at their own pace.
Stops for breath after about 100 metres, or after a few minutes on the flat.
Too breathless to leave the house, or breathless while dressing.

teach.note: Always ask what they could do a year ago and five years ago. The grade tells you where they are; the change tells you how fast they are getting there, and that is often the more useful number.

teach.heading: Separate orthopnoea from PND, they are not the same
teach.body: Both are breathlessness related to lying down, and students routinely merge them. The timing and the way the patient gets relief tell them apart.

rows: Wakes them 2 to 3 hours into sleep
Sits up, adds pillows, sleeps propped
Gets out of bed, sits with legs down, goes to a window
Blood shifts from the legs into the chest, and the diaphragm is pushed up
Reabsorbed fluid plus a depressed respiratory centre during sleep

teach.note: Neither is specific to the heart. Orthopnoea also occurs in severe COPD, gross ascites and marked obesity. It is the company it keeps that makes it cardiac.

teach.heading: The questions that separate the causes
points: How long: sudden over minutes suggests pneumothorax or embolism; days suggests infection or effusion; months to years suggests COPD, fibrosis or anaemia.
Constant or in attacks: episodic with triggers and diurnal variation points to asthma.
What brings it on and what relieves it, including inhalers.
Any chest pain, and whether it is pleuritic.
Orthopnoea, PND and ankle swelling, for the cardiac contribution.
Wheeze, cough, sputum, fever, weight loss, night sweats.
Occupation and exposures, including birds and biomass smoke.
teach.note: In COPD, ask specifically about arm work above shoulder height. It is disproportionately hard because those muscles are already being borrowed to breathe.

skill.hx.resp.cough_sputum.title: Cough and sputum
skill.hx.resp.cough_sputum.oneLine: Duration, timing, and what actually comes up
skill.hx.resp.cough_sputum.why: Cough with sputum on most days for three months in two consecutive years is the definition of chronic bronchitis. The character and volume of sputum separates chronic bronchitis from bronchiectasis, and a change in an established smoker's cough is a cardinal warning of lung cancer.

asks.text: How long have you had the cough? Months and years, and whether it is present most days.
Is it worse at any particular time, especially first thing in the morning?
Do you bring anything up? If so, roughly how much in a day, using a household measure such as a teaspoon or a cupful.
What colour is it, and has that changed recently?
Have you ever coughed up blood?
Has the character of your usual cough changed?

skill.hx.resp.cough_sputum.practice: Ask a partner to describe sputum volume without using the words 'a lot' or 'a little'. Practise offering household measures until you get a number you could write down.
pitfalls: Asking 'do you have a productive cough?', which most patients do not understand. Ask whether anything comes up.
Accepting a colour without asking whether it has changed, which is what indicates an exacerbation.
Failing to quantify volume, which is what separates chronic bronchitis from bronchiectasis.
Not asking specifically about haemoptysis, and not treating a change in a smoker's cough as a red flag.

probes.q: What is the clinical definition of chronic bronchitis?
probes.a: Cough productive of sputum on most days for three months of the year, for two consecutive years.

probes.q: A patient brings up a cupful of purulent sputum daily. Which diagnosis does volume alone raise?
probes.a: Bronchiectasis. Large-volume purulent sputum is out of keeping with uncomplicated chronic bronchitis.

probes.q: A 60-year-old smoker says his usual morning cough has changed over two months. Why does that matter?
probes.a: A change in the character of a chronic smoker's cough is a recognised presenting feature of bronchial carcinoma and warrants imaging, regardless of how long the cough has been present.

rubric.text: Establishes duration and whether present most days
Quantifies sputum volume with a usable measure
Asks about colour and any recent change
Asks specifically about haemoptysis

teach.heading: What a cough actually is
teach.body:
A cough is a sudden, forced push of air out of the lungs through the airways, loud enough to interrupt the normal rhythm of breathing.

It is a reflex, not a decision. Irritant receptors in the pharynx, larynx, large airways and lung tissue send signals up the vagus to the cough centre in the brainstem, which fires the diaphragm and the expiratory muscles.

points.d: You cannot cough properly without one.
Pressure builds behind it.
Against a closed glottis.
Air blasts out and carries secretions with it.

teach.note: This matters clinically: anything that weakens any one of those four steps gives you a weak, ineffective cough. That is why a patient with vocal cord palsy or weak respiratory muscles cannot clear their chest.

teach.heading: Ask the duration first, because it splits the differential
teach.body: Before anything else, find out how long the cough has been there. Duration alone divides the causes into three very different lists.

rows: Tracheobronchitis, pneumonia, acute-on-chronic bronchitis. Sudden onset: asthma, foreign body, whooping cough
COPD, asthma, TB, interstitial lung disease, lung cancer, occupational lung disease

teach.note: Chronic cigarette smoking is the single commonest cause of a chronic cough. Also remember the non-respiratory causes at every duration: reflux, heart failure, and ACE inhibitors.

teach.heading: Then ask what it sounds like
teach.body: The character of the cough is a real clue, and patients can usually demonstrate it if you ask them to.

rows: Pleural disease, interstitial disease, mediastinal lesions
Trachea compressed from outside, by a mass or an aneurysm
Recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy, so the glottis cannot close
Whooping cough, chronic bronchitis, asthma, foreign body
Heavy smoker, chronic pharyngitis or laryngitis

teach.note: A bovine cough is worth recognising on the spot. It means the cord cannot close, so the cough has no explosive phase, and it points you straight at a lesion on the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

teach.heading: If anything comes up, describe it properly
teach.body: Do not ask whether the cough is productive; most patients do not know what that means. Ask whether anything comes up when they cough, and then pin down three things: how much, what it looks like, and whether it smells.

points.d: Normal is only 10 to 15 mL a day and is swallowed unnoticed. Over 100 mL a day is bronchorrhoea. Offer household measures: a teaspoon, an eggcup, half a cup.

Mucoid and clear is chronic bronchitis or asthma. Purulent and yellow-green means infection. Rusty suggests pneumococcal pneumonia. Pink and frothy means pulmonary oedema. Currant-jelly and sticky suggests Klebsiella.
Foul-smelling sputum means anaerobes: think lung abscess or bronchiectasis.
Ask what is different from usual. A change in volume or colour is what defines an exacerbation.

teach.note: Two findings are close to diagnostic on their own. Sputum that settles into three layers, foam on top, mucus in the middle, thick pus at the bottom, is bronchiectasis. And sputum that only comes up in certain positions means a cavity or a dilated airway is draining when gravity allows it.

teach.heading: Always ask about blood, and mean it
teach.body:
Haemoptysis is coughing blood from below the vocal cords. It runs from a streak in the sputum to frank blood with no sputum at all, and it always needs explaining.

Ask it as a direct question. Patients often do not volunteer a small streak because they assume it came from the throat.

rows: Night sweats, weight loss, contact history
Medication effect or a clotting disorder

teach.note: Before calling it haemoptysis, make sure it was coughed and not vomited, and that it did not come from the nose or gums. Blood that is frothy and bright red with a cough is haemoptysis; dark blood with food and nausea is haematemesis.

skill.hx.resp.smoking.title: Smoking and inhaled exposure
skill.hx.resp.smoking.oneLine: Pack-years, and the exposures that are not tobacco
skill.hx.resp.smoking.why: Smoking is the dominant cause of COPD, and pack-years quantify the dose in a way that can be compared and recorded. But a substantial share of COPD worldwide, and a very large share in Indian women, is caused by biomass cooking fuel, which is missed entirely if the only question asked is about cigarettes.

asks.text: Do you smoke, or have you ever smoked? Include bidis, hookah and cannabis, not only cigarettes.
How many per day, and for how many years? Calculate pack-years: packs per day multiplied by years, where one pack is twenty cigarettes.
If they have stopped, when, and what were they smoking before?
What fuel is used for cooking at home, and is the kitchen ventilated? Ask about wood, dung cake, crop residue and coal.
Has anyone in the house smoked indoors?
Do you use an electronic cigarette or vape?

skill.hx.resp.smoking.practice: Calculate pack-years for three cases out loud: 20 a day for 30 years; 10 a day for 40 years; 40 a day for 15 years. All three are 30, 20 and 30 pack-years respectively.
pitfalls: Asking only about cigarettes. Bidis and hookah are frequently not volunteered as smoking.
Never asking about cooking fuel, which is the single commonest missed exposure in women with COPD in South Asia.
Recording 'chronic smoker' without a pack-year figure, which is unquantified and unusable.
Assuming a non-smoker cannot have COPD.

probes.q: How do you calculate pack-years?
probes.a: Packs smoked per day multiplied by years smoked, where a pack is twenty cigarettes.

probes.q: A 55-year-old woman who has never smoked has airflow obstruction. What exposure must you ask about?
probes.a: Biomass cooking fuel: wood, dung cake, crop residue or coal, particularly in an unventilated kitchen.

probes.q: Why does establishing pack-years matter beyond attributing cause?
probes.a: It quantifies risk for lung cancer as well as COPD, informs screening decisions, and gives a baseline against which cessation can be discussed and recorded.

rubric.text: Calculates and records pack-years
Asks about bidis, hookah and other forms
Asks about cooking fuel and indoor smoke

sources.locator: COPD, p.2249-2259 (cigarette smoke, biomass fuels, vaping)

skill.hx.resp.drug.title: Inhaler and drug history
skill.hx.resp.drug.oneLine: Not what was prescribed, but what is actually taken and how
skill.hx.resp.drug.why: In chronic airway disease the commonest reason for apparent treatment failure is not the drug, it is the device. A patient who cannot coordinate a metered dose inhaler is receiving almost nothing, however good the prescription. Asking the patient to demonstrate is worth more than any list of names.

asks.text: What inhalers do you use? Ask to see the actual devices rather than relying on names.
How many times a day, and how many puffs each time?
Which one do you use when you are breathless, and which every day?
Ask the patient to demonstrate their technique with the device or a placebo.
How many days in the last month did you miss it, and what gets in the way?
Have you needed steroid tablets or antibiotics for your chest in the last year, and how many times?
Do you use home oxygen or a nebuliser, and for how many hours a day?
Are you taking a beta blocker, and do you use any over-the-counter or traditional remedies?

skill.hx.resp.drug.practice: Ask someone to demonstrate a metered dose inhaler using a placebo device. Score them on shake, full exhalation, seal, slow deep inspiration with actuation, and a ten-second breath hold. Most people fail on at least two.
pitfalls: Recording inhaler names from the notes and never watching the patient use one.
Asking 'do you take it regularly?', which invites yes. Ask how many days were missed.
Not counting courses of oral steroids and antibiotics, which is the best available measure of exacerbation frequency and drives treatment decisions.
Missing that a reliever is being used many times a day, which is itself a marker of poor control.

probes.q: What is the most informative single question about inhaler use?
probes.a: Ask the patient to show you how they use it.

probes.q: Why count courses of oral steroids and antibiotics over the past year?
probes.a: Exacerbation frequency is the best predictor of future exacerbations and drives escalation of inhaled therapy.

probes.q: A COPD patient with ischaemic heart disease is on a beta blocker. Is that a problem?
probes.a: Cardioselective beta blockers are generally tolerated in COPD and their cardiac benefit usually outweighs the risk, so they should not be withheld reflexively. Non-selective agents are more likely to provoke bronchospasm. The decision is individualised and made with the treating clinician.

rubric.text: Identifies the actual devices in use
Asks the patient to demonstrate inhaler technique
Quantifies missed doses rather than asking if adherent
Counts steroid and antibiotic courses in the past year

skill.exam.resp.inspection.title: Inspection of the chest
skill.exam.resp.inspection.oneLine: Shape, movement, effort, and the signs that only exist before you touch
skill.exam.resp.inspection.why: Inspection carries more diagnostic weight in respiratory examination than any other step, and it is the one students hurry through. Hyperinflation, accessory muscle use, pursed-lip breathing and asymmetry of movement are all visible, and all are lost once the patient starts responding to your hands.

steps.text: With the patient at 45 degrees and the chest exposed, look from the foot of the bed and then from the side.
Note the shape: increased anteroposterior diameter (barrel chest), pectus deformity, kyphoscoliosis, or a flattened hemithorax.
Watch the movement for symmetry and for which part of the chest moves.
Look for accessory muscle use: sternocleidomastoid, scalenes, and the shoulders rising with each breath.
Look for pursed-lip breathing, and for indrawing of the lower intercostal spaces on inspiration (Hoover sign).
Look for scars, including small thoracoscopy and chest-drain scars in the axillae, and for dilated veins.

skill.exam.resp.inspection.normal: An anteroposterior diameter less than the transverse, symmetrical movement mainly of the lower chest, no accessory muscle use, quiet breathing through the nose or mouth without pursed lips.
skill.exam.resp.inspection.abnormal: Barrel-shaped chest with a raised anteroposterior diameter, reduced or asymmetrical movement, accessory muscle use, pursed-lip breathing, intercostal or supraclavicular indrawing, and paradoxical inward movement of the lower ribs on inspiration.
skill.exam.resp.inspection.significance: Barrel chest, accessory muscle use and pursed-lip breathing together indicate hyperinflation with airflow obstruction. Hoover sign, the inward movement of the lower costal margin on inspiration, occurs because a flattened diaphragm pulls the ribs in rather than lifting them out, and is a specific sign of severe hyperinflation.
skill.exam.resp.inspection.practice: Watch someone breathe for a full minute from the side. Identify which part of the chest moves most, and count how many of the six inspection items you can positively report.
pitfalls: Inspecting for three seconds before reaching for the chest. Most inspection findings need a full respiratory cycle or several.
Looking only from the front, so that anteroposterior diameter and shoulder movement are never appreciated.
Forgetting to look in the axillae and on the back for scars.
Describing a chest as barrel-shaped without comparing the anteroposterior and transverse diameters.

probes.q: What is Hoover sign?
probes.a: Paradoxical inward movement of the lower costal margin during inspiration.

probes.q: Why does pursed-lip breathing help a patient with airflow obstruction?
probes.a: It creates positive pressure in the airway during expiration, splinting open small airways that would otherwise collapse and trap gas.

probes.q: Explain the mechanism of Hoover sign.
probes.a: Severe hyperinflation flattens the diaphragm. A flat diaphragm contracting pulls the lower ribs inward instead of lifting them outward, reversing the normal bucket-handle movement.

rubric.text: Exposes and positions the patient adequately
Comments on chest shape and AP diameter
Comments on accessory muscle use and breathing pattern
Looks for scars front and back

skill.exam.resp.trachea.title: Tracheal position
skill.exam.resp.trachea.oneLine: One finger, gently, and warn the patient first
skill.exam.resp.trachea.why: Tracheal deviation localises upper mediastinal shift, and the direction distinguishes a process pulling the mediastinum (collapse, fibrosis) from one pushing it (large effusion, tension pneumothorax). It is uncomfortable if done badly, which is why technique matters as much as the finding.

steps.text: Warn the patient that this may be briefly uncomfortable, and ask them to look straight ahead with the neck relaxed.
Place the index finger in the suprasternal notch and feel gently for the trachea.
Compare the space between the trachea and the sternocleidomastoid heads on each side.
Assess the cricosternal distance, normally about three to four finger-breadths, as a measure of hyperinflation.
If shift is suspected, corroborate with the apex beat position.

skill.exam.resp.trachea.normal: Central trachea with equal spaces either side, and a cricosternal distance of three or more finger-breadths.
skill.exam.resp.trachea.abnormal: Deviation to one side, or a reduced cricosternal distance of two finger-breadths or less indicating hyperinflation with a low-lying trachea.
skill.exam.resp.trachea.significance: The trachea deviates towards collapse and fibrosis, and away from a large pleural effusion or a tension pneumothorax. In COPD the trachea stays central, but the cricosternal distance shortens and a tracheal tug may be seen because of hyperinflation.
skill.exam.resp.trachea.practice: Find the trachea on yourself using one finger only. Notice how little pressure is needed, then measure your own cricosternal distance in finger-breadths.
pitfalls: Using two or three fingers and pressing hard, which is painful and no more accurate.
Not warning the patient, which is the commonest reason a candidate is stopped in an examination.
Assessing with the head turned or the neck flexed, which displaces the trachea artificially.
Reporting deviation without checking the apex beat to corroborate mediastinal shift.

probes.q: How many fingers should you use to assess tracheal position?
probes.a: One.

probes.q: A large left pleural effusion. Which way does the trachea deviate?
probes.a: Away from the effusion, to the right.

probes.q: What is the cricosternal distance and what does a reduced distance mean?
probes.a: The distance between the cricoid cartilage and the suprasternal notch, normally three to four finger-breadths. A reduction to two or fewer indicates hyperinflation with a low-lying trachea.

rubric.text: Warns the patient before palpating
Uses a single finger with gentle pressure
Compares the space on both sides

skill.exam.resp.expansion.title: Chest expansion
skill.exam.resp.expansion.oneLine: Let your thumbs float, or you will measure your own hands
skill.exam.resp.expansion.why: Chest expansion quantifies how much the lung is actually moving and, more usefully, whether the two sides move equally. Asymmetry localises disease to the side that lags. The technique has one critical detail: the thumbs must be free of the chest wall, or they move with the skin and the sign disappears.

steps.text: For the upper chest, place your hands over the upper anterior chest with the fingers gripping the sides.
For the lower chest, grip the lower rib cage from behind or in front with the fingers, and bring the thumbs together in the midline.
Lift the thumbs slightly off the chest wall so they are free to move.
Ask the patient to take a deep breath in.
Watch the distance each thumb travels from the midline, and compare the two sides.
Repeat at the upper, middle and lower zones, and compare front with back.

skill.exam.resp.expansion.normal: Symmetrical movement, with each thumb moving about 2.5 to 5 cm from the midline on deep inspiration.
skill.exam.resp.expansion.abnormal: Reduced total expansion, or one thumb moving less than the other, indicating reduced movement on that side.
skill.exam.resp.expansion.significance: Asymmetrical expansion localises pathology to the lagging side, and is one of the earliest signs of a unilateral process such as effusion, consolidation, collapse or pneumothorax. Symmetrically reduced expansion suggests a diffuse process such as hyperinflation in COPD or interstitial fibrosis.
skill.exam.resp.expansion.practice: Assess a partner's lower chest expansion twice: once with the thumbs anchored to the skin, once with them floating. The difference in what you can see is the whole point of the technique.
pitfalls: Anchoring the thumbs to the chest wall, so they travel with the skin and no asymmetry can be seen. This is the single commonest technical error in the respiratory examination.
Assessing only one zone and reporting expansion as normal.
Not asking for a deep breath, or asking while the patient is mid-cycle.
Comparing sides using two different hand positions.

probes.q: Why must your thumbs be lifted off the chest wall?
probes.a: So they move freely with the chest rather than travelling with the skin, which is what makes asymmetry visible.

probes.q: The left thumb moves less than the right. Which side is diseased?
probes.a: The left, the lagging side.

probes.q: What does symmetrically reduced expansion suggest?
probes.a: A diffuse bilateral process such as hyperinflation in COPD, interstitial fibrosis, or a restrictive chest-wall or neuromuscular problem.

rubric.text: Lifts the thumbs clear of the chest wall
Assesses more than one zone
Explicitly compares the two sides
Instructs the patient to take a deep breath

skill.exam.resp.percussion.title: Percussion
skill.exam.resp.percussion.oneLine: Compare like with like, side to side, and move the pleximeter finger
skill.exam.resp.percussion.why: Percussion samples what lies immediately beneath the chest wall and separates air from fluid from solid. Its value is almost entirely comparative: an absolute note is hard to judge, but a difference between two matched points on opposite sides is unmistakable even to a beginner.

steps.text: Place the middle finger of your non-dominant hand flat against the chest wall, pressed firmly, in an intercostal space.
Strike the middle phalanx of that finger with the tip of your dominant middle finger, using a loose movement from the wrist.
Strike twice, then lift the finger away between sites.
Work from side to side at matched levels, not down one side and then the other.
Percuss the clavicle directly for the lung apex.
Include the axillae, and percuss the back with the patient's arms folded forward.

skill.exam.resp.percussion.normal: A resonant note throughout, with dullness over the cardiac area and the liver, and a normal area of cardiac and hepatic dullness.
skill.exam.resp.percussion.abnormal: Hyperresonance (increased air), dullness (consolidation, collapse, fibrosis), or stony dullness (pleural effusion). Loss of the normal areas of cardiac and hepatic dullness indicates hyperinflation.
skill.exam.resp.percussion.significance: Stony dullness at a base with reduced breath sounds is the classic effusion. Hyperresonance with loss of cardiac and liver dullness indicates hyperinflation, as in COPD, and marked unilateral hyperresonance with tracheal shift suggests pneumothorax.
skill.exam.resp.percussion.practice: Percuss your own thigh, then your own inflated cheek, then a table. Those three notes are roughly dull, resonant and flat. Then percuss a partner's chest side to side and find the liver edge.
pitfalls: Percussing down one side completely and then the other, which loses the comparison that gives the technique its power.
Leaving the pleximeter finger loosely applied, which damps the note.
Percussing over the scapula or the sternum and reporting dullness.
Forgetting the axillae, where a surprising amount of lung lies.
Percussing with a stiff arm rather than a loose wrist.

probes.q: In which direction should you percuss?
probes.a: Side to side at matched levels, comparing the two sides.

probes.q: What does stony dullness at the left base suggest?
probes.a: A pleural effusion.

probes.q: Why is loss of cardiac and hepatic dullness significant in COPD?
probes.a: Hyperinflated lung expands over the heart and liver, replacing the normally dull areas with resonant lung. It is a bedside sign of hyperinflation.

rubric.text: Uses correct pleximeter placement and a loose wrist
Percusses side to side comparing matched levels
Includes apices, axillae and the back

skill.exam.resp.auscultation.title: Auscultation: breath sounds
skill.exam.resp.auscultation.oneLine: Quality first, then intensity, then what is added
skill.exam.resp.auscultation.why: Breath sounds tell you whether air is reaching the alveoli and whether the lung between the alveoli and your stethoscope conducts sound normally. Reduced breath sounds and bronchial breathing are not degrees of the same thing; they mean opposite things about the underlying lung.

steps.text: Ask the patient to breathe deeply through an open mouth.
Use the diaphragm, applied firmly, and compare side to side at matched levels.
Listen through a full inspiration and expiration at each site.
Judge the quality first: vesicular or bronchial.
Then judge the intensity, comparing the two sides.
Cover apices, axillae, and the back, and listen for at least six sites on each side.

skill.exam.resp.auscultation.normal: Vesicular breath sounds: a rustling inspiratory sound continuing without pause into a shorter, quieter expiration, of equal intensity on both sides.
skill.exam.resp.auscultation.abnormal: Reduced or absent breath sounds, or bronchial breathing, which is a hollow blowing sound with a gap between inspiration and expiration and an expiratory phase as long and as loud as inspiration.
skill.exam.resp.auscultation.significance: Reduced breath sounds occur when air entry is poor or when air or fluid separates the lung from the chest wall, as in COPD, effusion or pneumothorax. Bronchial breathing occurs when consolidated lung conducts central airway sounds to the surface, and is the classic sign of consolidation.
skill.exam.resp.auscultation.practice: Listen to a partner's chest at six matched pairs of sites. At each pair, say aloud whether the sounds are equal before moving on. Naming it forces the comparison.
pitfalls: Listening through only part of a respiratory cycle, so expiration is never actually heard.
Using the bell rather than the diaphragm for breath sounds.
Listening over clothing.
Letting the patient hyperventilate to the point of dizziness. Pause and let them rest.
Reporting 'reduced air entry bilaterally' without comparing sides or considering that quiet breath sounds may simply reflect shallow breathing.

probes.q: Which part of the stethoscope do you use for breath sounds?
probes.a: The diaphragm.

probes.q: How does bronchial breathing differ from vesicular?
probes.a: It is hollow and blowing, with a pause between inspiration and expiration, and the expiratory phase is as long and as loud as the inspiratory phase.

probes.q: Why does consolidated lung produce bronchial breathing?
probes.a: Solid lung conducts sound better than air-filled lung, so the sounds generated in the large central airways are transmitted to the chest wall instead of being filtered out.

probes.q: A severe asthmatic has a silent chest. Is that reassuring?
probes.a: No. A silent chest means airflow is too low to generate sound and is a sign of life-threatening obstruction requiring immediate senior and critical-care input.

rubric.text: Instructs the patient to breathe deeply through the mouth
Comments on the quality of breath sounds
Compares side to side at matched levels
Auscultates apices, axillae and the back

skill.exam.resp.added_sounds.title: Added sounds
skill.exam.resp.added_sounds.oneLine: Wheeze, crackles and rub, and the timing that identifies each
skill.exam.resp.added_sounds.why: Added sounds carry specific diagnostic information, but only when timed within the respiratory cycle. Early inspiratory crackles mean something different from late inspiratory crackles; a wheeze that is monophonic means something different from one that is polyphonic. Reporting 'crepitations present' discards nearly all of that information.

steps.text: At each auscultation site, listen specifically for sounds added to the breath sounds.
For any crackle, note whether it is early or late in inspiration, and whether it is fine or coarse.
For any wheeze, note whether it is inspiratory or expiratory, and whether it is a single note (monophonic) or many notes together (polyphonic).
Ask the patient to cough, and listen again. Crackles that clear with coughing are usually secretions.
Listen for a pleural rub: a creaking sound present in both phases, unaffected by coughing, and often painful.

skill.exam.resp.added_sounds.abnormal: Wheeze (a musical continuous sound, usually expiratory), crackles (discontinuous popping sounds, fine or coarse, early or late in inspiration), or a pleural rub.
skill.exam.resp.added_sounds.significance: Polyphonic expiratory wheeze indicates diffuse airflow obstruction, as in COPD and asthma. A fixed monophonic wheeze suggests a single narrowed airway and raises tumour or foreign body. Early coarse crackles that change with coughing suggest airway secretions as in COPD and bronchiectasis, whereas fine late inspiratory crackles that do not clear suggest pulmonary fibrosis or pulmonary oedema.
skill.exam.resp.added_sounds.practice: Listen to a partner and, at each site, say aloud either 'no added sounds' or the full description with timing. Practise refusing to say 'crepitations' without a qualifier.
pitfalls: Recording 'crepitations' or 'added sounds present' with no timing, character or distribution, which conveys almost nothing.
Not asking the patient to cough, which is what separates secretions from fixed pathology.
Assuming all wheeze is asthma or COPD, and so missing a fixed monophonic wheeze from an obstructing tumour.
Mistaking transmitted upper airway sounds for wheeze. Listen at the mouth and over the trachea to compare.

probes.q: In which phase of respiration is wheeze usually heard in airflow obstruction?
probes.a: Expiration.

probes.q: What is the significance of a fixed monophonic wheeze?
probes.a: It suggests narrowing of a single large airway, raising the possibility of tumour or a foreign body, and warrants imaging and bronchoscopy.

probes.q: How do crackles in COPD differ from those in pulmonary fibrosis?
probes.a: COPD gives early, coarse crackles that often change or clear with coughing because they arise from secretions. Fibrosis gives fine, late inspiratory crackles that do not clear with coughing.

rubric.text: Times added sounds within the respiratory cycle
Describes character (fine/coarse, mono/polyphonic)
Asks the patient to cough and re-auscultates

skill.exam.resp.vocal_resonance.title: Vocal resonance and fremitus
skill.exam.resp.vocal_resonance.oneLine: The same physiology, once with the stethoscope and once with the hand
skill.exam.resp.vocal_resonance.why: Voice transmission distinguishes solid lung from fluid and from air, and it confirms what percussion and auscultation have already suggested. Consolidated lung conducts the voice better; fluid and air conduct it worse. Doing it after percussion turns a suspicion into a confirmed pattern.

steps.text: For vocal resonance, place the stethoscope diaphragm on the chest and ask the patient to say a repeated phrase such as ninety-nine or a local equivalent.
Compare the loudness at matched sites on both sides.
For tactile fremitus, use the ulnar border or the flat of the hand in the same positions while the patient repeats the phrase.
Where resonance is increased, test for whispering pectoriloquy by asking the patient to whisper the phrase.
Correlate with the percussion note and the breath sounds at the same site.

skill.exam.resp.vocal_resonance.normal: Equal, muffled voice sounds on both sides, with the words indistinct.
skill.exam.resp.vocal_resonance.abnormal: Increased resonance and fremitus with clearly audible whispered speech (whispering pectoriloquy) over consolidation, or reduced resonance and fremitus over an effusion or pneumothorax.
skill.exam.resp.vocal_resonance.significance: Increased vocal resonance with bronchial breathing and a dull percussion note is the complete picture of consolidation. Reduced resonance with stony dullness and absent breath sounds is the complete picture of a pleural effusion. In COPD, vocal resonance is usually reduced in proportion to the reduced breath sounds.
skill.exam.resp.vocal_resonance.practice: Test vocal resonance on a partner at six matched pairs. Then have them whisper and notice how completely indistinct normal whispered speech is through healthy lung.
pitfalls: Testing at unmatched sites, so a difference in position is mistaken for a difference in the lung.
Using a phrase the patient does not understand or cannot say comfortably. Any repeatable phrase works.
Reporting vocal resonance in isolation rather than combining it with percussion and breath sounds into a pattern.
Forgetting that both consolidation and effusion may coexist, giving a mixed picture.

probes.q: What happens to vocal resonance over consolidation?
probes.a: It is increased.

probes.q: Give the full triad of percussion, breath sounds and vocal resonance for a pleural effusion.
probes.a: Stony dull percussion note, absent or reduced breath sounds, and reduced vocal resonance.

probes.q: Why does consolidated lung transmit the voice better than normal lung?
probes.a: Air-filled alveoli scatter and filter sound. When alveoli fill with exudate the lung becomes a better conducting medium, so higher-frequency voice components reach the chest wall.

rubric.text: Tests at matched sites on both sides
Uses either vocal resonance or tactile fremitus competently
Integrates the finding with percussion and auscultation

skill.exam.resp.corpulmonale.title: Looking for cor pulmonale
skill.exam.resp.corpulmonale.oneLine: The right heart failing because of the lung, whatever the lung disease is
skill.exam.resp.corpulmonale.why: Cor pulmonale marks a change in prognosis and in management, and every one of its signs is elicited during examinations students already know how to do. It is missed not because it is subtle but because nobody goes looking for it in a respiratory case. It complicates any chronic lung disease severe enough to cause sustained hypoxaemia, not COPD alone.

steps.text: Look at the JVP with the patient at 45 degrees, and identify its upper level relative to the sternal angle.
Feel for a parasternal (right ventricular) heave with the heel of the hand at the left sternal edge.
Listen at the pulmonary area for a loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound.
Listen for a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge that increases on inspiration, indicating functional tricuspid regurgitation.
Palpate for a pulsatile, tender liver edge and check for ascites.
Check for bilateral dependent pitting oedema, and the sacrum in a bed-bound patient.

skill.exam.resp.corpulmonale.normal: JVP not raised, no parasternal heave, normal second heart sound, no murmur, no hepatomegaly, no oedema.
skill.exam.resp.corpulmonale.abnormal: Raised JVP, parasternal heave, loud P2, tricuspid regurgitation murmur, tender pulsatile hepatomegaly and dependent pitting oedema.
skill.exam.resp.corpulmonale.significance: These findings together indicate right ventricular pressure overload and failure secondary to chronic lung disease. Their presence marks advanced disease, worsens prognosis, and prompts assessment for long-term oxygen therapy where criteria are met.
skill.exam.resp.corpulmonale.practice: On any patient with chronic lung disease, deliberately add the four right-heart steps to the end of your respiratory examination until it becomes automatic.
pitfalls: Not looking, because the case was labelled respiratory.
Assessing the JVP at the wrong angle, which makes it uninterpretable.
Attributing oedema to immobility without examining the JVP and the right ventricle.
Missing that a hyperinflated chest displaces the liver downwards, so a palpable liver edge is not by itself hepatomegaly. Percuss the upper border before calling it enlarged.

probes.q: Where do you feel for a right ventricular heave?
probes.a: At the left sternal edge, with the heel of the hand.

probes.q: A COPD patient has a palpable liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin. Is that hepatomegaly?
probes.a: Not necessarily. Hyperinflation pushes the liver down, so the lower edge is palpable with a normal-sized liver. Percuss the upper border and measure the span before calling it enlarged.

probes.q: Why does chronic hypoxaemia cause right heart failure?
probes.a: Alveolar hypoxia causes pulmonary arteriolar vasoconstriction. Sustained, this raises pulmonary vascular resistance and pulmonary artery pressure, imposing a pressure load on the right ventricle which hypertrophies and eventually fails.

rubric.text: Assesses the JVP at 45 degrees
Palpates for a parasternal heave
Listens for a loud P2
Examines the liver and checks for oedema

skill.resp.patterns.title: Reading the pattern: which disease is this?
skill.resp.patterns.oneLine: Four findings separate almost every respiratory case
skill.resp.patterns.why: A list of signs is not a diagnosis. What turns findings into a disease is the PATTERN they make, and in the chest four findings do almost all of the work: where the trachea points, the percussion note, the breath sounds, and the vocal resonance. Learn the pattern and you can name the pathology at the bedside before any imaging.

teach.heading: Four findings, in this order
teach.body:
Every respiratory case comes down to the same four questions. Ask them in this order and the answer usually falls out.

Where is the mediastinum? What is the percussion note? What are the breath sounds? What happens to the voice?
teach.note: Percussion and vocal resonance are the pair that separate the two commonest confusions: consolidation from effusion, and effusion from collapse.

teach.heading: 1. Which way does the mediastinum move
teach.body: Something that takes up space pushes it away. Something that loses volume pulls it towards.
teach.note: This is the single most useful discriminator you have. A dull hemithorax with the trachea PULLED towards it is collapse, not effusion, and usually means something is obstructing a bronchus.

teach.heading: 2. The percussion note

rows: Hyperresonant, with cardiac and liver dullness lost

teach.note: Stony dullness is a different quality, not just more dullness. Percuss your own thigh and then a full effusion and you will not forget it.

teach.heading: 3. Breath sounds and 4. the voice, together
teach.body: These two move in the same direction, and the direction is the answer. Solid lung CONDUCTS sound better, so both increase. Fluid or air BLOCKS it, so both fall.
teach.note: Consolidation is the ONLY common cause where the voice gets LOUDER. If percussion is dull and the voice is louder, it is consolidation; if dull and quieter, think fluid or collapse.

points.d: Both dull, both quiet. The trachea decides: pushed away is fluid, pulled towards is collapse.
Both dull. The voice decides: louder is consolidation, quieter is fluid.

points.t: Bronchial breathing just ABOVE an effusion.
points.d: Compressed but still aerated lung sits above the fluid and conducts sound. Heard at the upper border it is expected; heard over the fluid it means consolidation.

pitfalls: Naming a disease from one finding. It is the combination that is diagnostic.
Forgetting to check the apex beat when the trachea suggests a shift. The two should agree.
Calling any dullness stony. Stony dullness is a distinct quality and it means fluid.

probes.q: A stony dull left base with absent breath sounds and reduced vocal resonance. What is it?
probes.a: A left pleural effusion.

probes.q: Dull percussion note but the voice is LOUDER. What does that tell you?
probes.a: Consolidation. Solid lung conducts the voice better; fluid and collapse both reduce it.

probes.q: A dull hemithorax with the trachea PULLED towards it. Effusion or collapse, and why does it matter?
probes.a: Collapse, because a volume-losing process pulls the mediastinum towards it while an effusion pushes it away. It matters because collapse usually means an obstructing lesion and needs imaging and often bronchoscopy.

probes.q: Why do breath sounds and vocal resonance always move in the same direction?
probes.a: Both depend on how well the lung between the airway and your stethoscope conducts sound. Solid lung conducts better so both rise; interposed fluid or air conducts worse so both fall.

skill.resp.diagnosis_format.title: Stating a respiratory diagnosis
skill.resp.diagnosis_format.oneLine: Anatomical, then pathological, then aetiological, then complications
skill.resp.diagnosis_format.why: Saying 'pleural effusion' answers a quarter of the question. A respiratory diagnosis has four parts, and examiners ask for all four because each one changes what happens to the patient next: where it is, what it is, why it happened, and what it has cost them.

teach.heading: The four parts, in order

points.d: Which side, which lobe, lung or pleura. Right upper lobe, left pleural space, bilateral.
What the process is. Consolidation, collapse, fibrosis, effusion, pneumothorax, obstructive or restrictive disease.
Why. Tuberculosis, malignancy, smoking, occupation, trauma.
What it has caused. Respiratory failure, and which type. Cor pulmonale.

teach.note: Say all four even when one is uncertain. 'Aetiology not yet established, tuberculosis to be excluded' is a real answer and shows you know the slot exists.

teach.heading: Three worked examples
points: Right upper lobe fibrosis, post-tubercular in origin, with no evidence of respiratory failure or cor pulmonale.
Bilateral obstructive lung disease, emphysema secondary to smoking, with type 2 respiratory failure and cor pulmonale.
Left-sided pleural effusion secondary to malignancy, with no respiratory failure or cor pulmonale.
teach.note: Notice that each one ends by explicitly EXCLUDING the complications. Saying 'no evidence of respiratory failure or cor pulmonale' tells the examiner you looked, which is worth as much as finding it.

teach.heading: Why the aetiology slot changes management
teach.body:
The same effusion is drained, treated with antituberculosis therapy, or managed with pleurodesis depending only on the aetiology.

That is why a diagnosis that stops at the pathology is incomplete: it names the finding but gives nobody a plan.

pitfalls: Stopping at the pathological diagnosis, which names the finding but not the patient.
Skipping the complications, so respiratory failure or cor pulmonale goes unstated.
Guessing an aetiology to fill the slot. Say what you would do to establish it instead.

probes.q: Name the four parts of a respiratory diagnosis.
probes.a: Anatomical, pathological, aetiological, and complications.

probes.q: State a full diagnosis for a smoker with emphysema, type 2 failure and cor pulmonale.
probes.a: Bilateral obstructive lung disease, emphysema secondary to smoking, with type 2 respiratory failure and cor pulmonale.

probes.q: Why does the aetiological part matter so much?
probes.a: Because it determines management. The same effusion is drained, treated for tuberculosis, or managed with pleurodesis depending entirely on why it is there.
